content: The process of measuring a patient's temperature is a fundamental component of a comprehensive clinical examination. Sustained deviations from this range, whether as hyperthermia (elevated temperature) or hypothermia (reduced temperature), are incompatible with life. It is important to note that body temperature naturally fluctuates depending on the time of day and physiological conditions, as governed by thermoregulation.8 to 98.6°F). Rectal temperature readings are generally 0.5°C (0.5°C (0.9°F) lower. A temperature exceeding 38°C (100°F) is classified as a fever. It is worth noting that consuming hot or cold beverages can temporarily alter oral temperature readings for up to 30 minutes. Consequently, various indirect methods are employed. These risks have been mitigated by the introduction of electronic thermometers, which are constructed from solid plastic and utilize a thermocouple sensor for temperature detection. Plastic thermometer strips, which change color when placed on the forehead, provide an approximate local temperature reading. However, these readings are significantly influenced by ambient air temperature and local blood circulation. Measuring temperature under the armpit is less affected by environmental air temperature but may still deviate from true core temperature due to variations in blood flow. Recently, tympanic (ear) thermometers have gained popularity, as the eardrum is thought to closely reflect core body temperature. These devices detect infrared heat emitted by the tympanic membrane and provide a reading within one second, making them particularly useful for pediatric patients. It is suggested that changes in core body temperature are detected more rapidly and accurately in the ear than at other sites. While the digital display of ear thermometers is easier to interpret than traditional thermometer markings, concerns have been raised about their accuracy in home settings. Oral temperature readings can be affected by recent food or drink intake, as well as breathing patterns. Skin temperature readings, such as those taken under the arm or on the forehead, are not always reliable indicators of core body temperature, particularly during critical periods of temperature fluctuation. This is because the skin plays a role in thermoregulation. For instance, during the onset of fever, shivering may occur as the body attempts to conserve heat, leading to discrepancies between skin and core temperatures. Additionally, skin temperature readings can be influenced by factors such as antipyretic medications, clothing, and external environmental conditions.
